claim: Acetate concentrations are significantly increased in diabetes mellitus patients compared to healthy volunteers.
source: We observed a significant increase of acetate in parallel with the canonical elevation of ketone bodies (3-HB and AcAc) and serum glucose in diabetes mellitus patients as compared with healthy controls (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1A comparing diabetes patients (n=17) to healthy controls (n=8).

claim: Serum acetate levels are dramatically elevated in STZ-induced type I diabetic C57BL/6 mice.
source: We then detected acetate in mouse models and found that the levels of serum acetate and ketone bodies were dramatically elevated to the same extent in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type I diabetic C57BL/6 (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from STZ-induced diabetic mice shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Serum acetate levels are dramatically elevated in STZ-induced type I diabetic BALB/c mice.
source: We then detected acetate in mouse models and found that the levels of serum acetate and ketone bodies were dramatically elevated to the same extent in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type I diabetic C57BL/6 (Figure 1B) and BALB/c mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from STZ-induced diabetic BALB/c mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Serum acetate levels are elevated in type II diabetic db/db mice.
source: We then detected acetate in mouse models and found that the levels of serum acetate and ketone bodies were dramatically elevated to the same extent in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type I diabetic C57BL/6 (Figure 1B) and BALB/c mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) as in type II diabetic db/db mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from db/db mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Starvation leads to a marked increase in serum acetate levels in normal C57BL/6 mice.
source: As expected, starvation also leads to a marked decrease in serum glucose concentration and an increase in serum acetate and ketone body levels in normal C57BL/6 (Figure 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from starved C57BL/6 mice shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Starvation leads to a marked increase in serum acetate levels in normal BALB/c mice.
source: As expected, starvation also leads to a marked decrease in serum glucose concentration and an increase in serum acetate and ketone body levels in normal C57BL/6 (Figure 1C) and BALB/c mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from starved BALB/c mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Serum acetate is boosted to the same extent as canonical ketone bodies under energy stresses including diabetes mellitus and starvation.
source: These data demonstrate that serum acetate is boosted to the same extent as canonical ketone bodies under energy stresses including those that occur with diabetes mellitus and starvation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing parallel increases in acetate and ketone bodies.

claim: Antibiotic pre-treatment does not significantly affect starvation-induced acetate production.
source: We observed that antibiotic pre-treatment failed to obviously affect the production of acetate that was induced by either starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from antibiotic-treated mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Antibiotic pre-treatment does not significantly affect diabetes-induced acetate production.
source: We observed that antibiotic pre-treatment failed to obviously affect the production of acetate that was induced by either starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B) or diabetes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from antibiotic-treated diabetic mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Energy stress-induced acetate is mainly produced endogenously rather than by gut microbiota.
source: We observed that antibiotic pre-treatment failed to obviously affect the production of acetate that was induced by either starvation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B) or diabetes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), demonstrating that ES-acetate is mainly produced endogenously.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from antibiotic treatment experiments that eliminated gut microbiota.

claim: Mammalian cells secrete different amounts of acetate into culture medium.
source: Next we used nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B) and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D) to detect the acetate that was secreted into the culture medium by several cell lines, and found that these cells showed different ability in producing acetate.
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR and GC-MS measurements of acetate in cell culture medium.

claim: Acetate is derived from glucose in mammalian cells supplied with abundant nutrients.
source: Consistently, Liu et al., 2018 reported that acetate is derived from glucose in mammalian cells supplied with abundant nutrients.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: 36.6% of acetate produced by cells cultured with U-13C-glucose is derived from nutrients other than glucose.
source: Interestingly, we also observed the production of 36.6% of non-U-13C-acetate, indicating that this proportion of acetate is derived from nutrients other than glucose (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by NMR data showing non-U-13C-acetate production in cells cultured with U-13C-glucose.

claim: Supplementation with free fatty acids significantly increases acetate production in cultured cells.
source: After different cells were cultured in Hanks' balanced salt solutions (HBSS, free of glucose, fatty acids and amino acids) supplemented with FFAs or amino acids for 20 hr, supplementation with FFAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D, E) rather than amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) significantly increased acetate levels, suggesting a major contribution of FFAs to acetate production.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing FFA and amino acid supplementation effects on acetate production.

claim: Supplementation with amino acids does not significantly increase acetate production in cultured cells.
source: After different cells were cultured in Hanks' balanced salt solutions (HBSS, free of glucose, fatty acids and amino acids) supplemented with FFAs or amino acids for 20 hr, supplementation with FFAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D, E) rather than amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) significantly increased acetate levels
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant effect of amino acid supplementation on acetate production.

claim: Free fatty acids are a major contributor to acetate production in cultured cells.
source: After different cells were cultured in Hanks' balanced salt solutions (HBSS, free of glucose, fatty acids and amino acids) supplemented with FFAs or amino acids for 20 hr, supplementation with FFAs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D, E) rather than amino acids (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) significantly increased acetate levels, suggesting a major contribution of FFAs to acetate production.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data showing FFA supplementation increases acetate production.

claim: Cell lines display different abilities to convert palmitate to acetate.
source: To confirm this observation, a series of widely used cell lines and mouse primary hepatocytes (MPHs) were cultured in HBSS supplemented with U-13C-palmitate, before secreted U-13C-acetate was measured (Figure 2A). These cell lines displayed quite different abilities to convert palmitate to acetate
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing varying levels of U-13C-acetate production from U-13C-palmitate across different cell lines.

claim: Cell lines can be divided into FFA-derived acetate-producing cells (FDAPCs) and no-FFA-derived acetate-producing cells (NFDAPCs).
source: These cell lines displayed quite different abilities to convert palmitate to acetate, and were accordingly divided into FFA-derived acetate-producing cells (FDAPCs: LO2, MPH, AML12, etc.) and no-FFA-derived acetate-producing cells (NFDAPCs: HEK-293T, Huh7, etc.).
evidence: The claim is based on classification of cell lines according to their ability to produce acetate from FFAs.

claim: FFA-derived acetate-producing cells secrete U-13C-acetate in a dose-dependent manner with U-13C-palmitate supplementation.
source: All of the FDAPCs secreted U-13C-acetate in a manner that was dependent on the dose of U-13C-palmitate supplementation (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent acetate production in MPH, LO2, and AML12 cells.

claim: High-fat diet induces a significant increase in acetate production in normal mice.
source: We also observed that high-fat diet induced a significant increase in acetate production in both normal and STZ-induced diabetic mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mice fed a high-fat diet shown in Figure 2E.

claim: High-fat diet induces a significant increase in acetate production in STZ-induced diabetic mice.
source: We also observed that high-fat diet induced a significant increase in acetate production in both normal and STZ-induced diabetic mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from STZ-induced diabetic mice fed a high-fat diet shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Acetate can be derived from free fatty acids in energy stress conditions.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that acetate can be derived from FFAs in energy stress conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experiments showing FFA-derived acetate production.

claim: The expression of Acot1/2/8/12 is upregulated significantly in mouse liver after 24 hr of fasting.
source: We next analyzed the GEO database and found out that the expression of Acot1/2/8/12 is upregulated significantly alongside the increase of β-oxidation and ketogenesis in mice liver after 24 hr of fasting (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq analysis data from Goldstein et al., 2017 shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Overexpression of ACOT8 in HEK-293T cells results in large amounts of acetate production.
source: To determine which ACOT is responsible for ES-acetate production, we overexpressed a series of ACOTs in HEK-293T cells and observed large amount of acetate production when either ACOT8 or ACOT12 was overexpressed (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ACOT overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Overexpression of ACOT12 in HEK-293T cells results in large amounts of acetate production.
source: To determine which ACOT is responsible for ES-acetate production, we overexpressed a series of ACOTs in HEK-293T cells and observed large amount of acetate production when either ACOT8 or ACOT12 was overexpressed (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from ACOT overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ACOT8 and ACOT12 are involved in energy stress-induced acetate production.
source: To determine which ACOT is responsible for ES-acetate production, we overexpressed a series of ACOTs in HEK-293T cells and observed large amount of acetate production when either ACOT8 or ACOT12 was overexpressed (Figure 3B), indicating that these two ACOTs are involved in ES-acetate production.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from overexpression experiments showing ACOT8 and ACOT12 increase acetate production.

claim: Acot12 protein levels are upregulated robustly in the livers of starved mice.
source: Consistently, the protein levels of both Acot12 and Acot8 are upregulated robustly in the livers of either starved mice or STZ-induced type I diabetic mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).

claim: Acot12 protein levels are upregulated robustly in the livers of STZ-induced type I diabetic mice.

evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from STZ-induced diabetic mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C.

source: Furthermore, when ACOT12 and ACOT8 were separately overexpressed in NFDAPCs HEK-293T and Huh7, FFA-derived acetate was significantly increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, E).

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing enzyme activity-dead mutants do not increase acetate production in Figure 3C.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from wildtype ACOT8 overexpression in Huh7 cells shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of ACOT12 in mouse primary hepatocytes diminishes U-13C-acetate production.
source: By contrast, knockdown (KD) of ACOT12 or ACOT8 in FDAPCs MPH (Figure 3E, F) and LO2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, G) diminished U-13C-acetate production.

claim: Knockdown of ACOT8 in mouse primary hepatocytes diminishes U-13C-acetate production.

claim: ACOT12 and ACOT8 are responsible for energy stress-induced acetate production.
source: These data reveal that ACOT12 and ACOT8 are responsible for ES-acetate production.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from overexpression and knockdown experiments showing ACOT12 and ACOT8 regulate acetate production.

claim: ACOT12 is mainly expressed in human liver together with genes encoding ketogenic enzymes.
source: ACOT12 is mainly expressed in human liver together with genes encoding ketogenic enzymes (HMGCS2, HMGCSL, ACAT1, and BDH1), whereas ACOT8 is expressed ubiquitously at a relative high level in most tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GTEx database analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACOT8 is expressed ubiquitously at a relatively high level in most human tissues.
source: ACOT12 is mainly expressed in human liver together with genes encoding ketogenic enzymes (HMGCS2, HMGCSL, ACAT1, and BDH1), whereas ACOT8 is expressed ubiquitously at a relative high level in most tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by GTEx database analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Acot12 is expressed mainly in mouse liver and kidney.
source: Acot12 is also expressed mainly in mouse liver and kidney, whereas Acot8 seems to be expressed at a much lower level in nearly all of the mouse tissues examined (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GEO database analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Acot8 is expressed at a much lower level in nearly all mouse tissues examined.
source: Acot12 is also expressed mainly in mouse liver and kidney, whereas Acot8 seems to be expressed at a much lower level in nearly all of the mouse tissues examined (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by GEO database analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: High levels of both Acot12 and Acot8 proteins are present in mouse liver and kidney.
source: Differing from their mRNA expression patterns in the GEO database, we observed high levels of both Acot12 and Acot8 proteins in mouse liver and kidney (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data from mouse tissues shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of Acot12 dramatically abolishes acetate production in starved C57BL/6 mice.
source: Consistently, adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of either Acot12 or Acot8 dramatically abolished acetate production by starved or diabetic C57BL/6 mice (Figure 4A–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from liver-specific Acot12 knockdown in starved mice shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of Acot8 dramatically abolishes acetate production in starved C57BL/6 mice.
source: Consistently, adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of either Acot12 or Acot8 dramatically abolished acetate production by starved or diabetic C57BL/6 mice (Figure 4A–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from liver-specific Acot8 knockdown in starved mice shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of Acot12 dramatically abolishes acetate production in diabetic C57BL/6 mice.
source: Consistently, adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of either Acot12 or Acot8 dramatically abolished acetate production by starved or diabetic C57BL/6 mice (Figure 4A–F)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from liver-specific Acot12 knockdown in diabetic mice shown in Figure 4A–F.

claim: Adenovirus-mediated liver-targeted knockdown of Acot8 dramatically abolishes acetate production in diabetic C57BL/6 mice.

claim: Conditional deletion of Acot12 in liver dramatically decreases acetate production in starved mice.

claim: Conditional deletion of Acot8 in liver dramatically decreases acetate production in starved mice.

claim: The liver is the main organ responsible for energy stress-induced acetate production.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from liver-specific knockdown and knockout experiments showing dramatic reduction in acetate production.

claim: U-13C-acetate derived from U-13C-palmitate in glucose-free HBSS is diminished by replenishment of glucose.

claim: Glucose is preferable to fatty acids as an energy source.

evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge and inference from experimental data showing glucose suppresses fatty acid-derived acetate production.

claim: Hepatic ACOT12 and ACOT8 are induced and responsible for energy stress-induced acetate production in diabetes mellitus and during starvation.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple experiments showing ACOT12 and ACOT8 upregulation and their role in acetate production during energy stress.
